observation: No published study applies Heer & Robertson-style object-constancy animated transitions to natural-language text reflow; charts have stable per-mark identity to animate between states, but L3 prose is not derived from L2 by a simple transformation, so there is no natural sentence-level correspondence to animate.
claim: No validated text-morphing transition exists for level changes; the honest options are a hard cut, a crossfade, or FLIP-style animation of only the elements with real cross-level identity (headings), with prose body crossfading.
mechanism: Object constancy requires a 1:1 mapping between before/after visual elements, which chart marks have and generated summary prose does not.
population: general (chart-transition research; no equivalent text-reflow study found)
context: controlled chart-animation experiments; text-transition design is a synthesis, not a finding

implications.text: Animate headings/node boundaries with FLIP-style movement (they have real identity continuity); crossfade prose body content (~150-250ms); disable all motion under prefers-reduced-motion.

observation: Workflowy and Logseq independently converged on the same pattern: zooming into a bullet/block collapses ancestors into a clickable breadcrumb bar, not into nothing; Workflowy's own design retrospective found that when the breadcrumb was hidden/truncated, users lost the 'bigger picture' workflow it was built for.
claim: The ancestor chain in Riemann's zoom dial should collapse into a persistent, clickable breadcrumb when it leaves the viewport, not disappear.
mechanism: A breadcrumb doing its orientation job is load-bearing, not decorative; two independently-built products converged on the same shipped mechanism.
population: general knowledge-worker/outliner users (product design retrospective, not controlled study)

implications.text: Render a fixed breadcrumb strip above content showing L0 gist → active ancestors → 'you are here', each segment clickable to re-center the dial.

observation: Marshall & Shipman's VIKI/spatial-hypertext work (1994-95) found that visual/spatial arrangement lets people express emerging, ambiguous, partial structure they can't or won't commit to formal categories for, without forcing early commitment to formal structure.
claim: A future spatial view should tolerate a half-organized state indefinitely rather than nudging users toward a 'finished' canvas.
mechanism: Forcing premature formal structure blocks people from expressing genuinely uncertain or evolving relationships between content.

implications.text: Any user-adjustable layer on top of the auto-generated tree layout should tolerate ambiguous, partial arrangement rather than requiring users to formally commit to structure.

observation: Every infinite-canvas product examined (Muse, Heptabase, Scapple, tldraw, Kinopio) converges on constraining the canvas with an underlying structured layer (cards/notes independent of position) rather than trusting position alone; Scapple's own maker explicitly scopes it as unsuited to organizing an entire book.
claim: If Riemann's tree is ever rendered as a canvas, node identity/content/relationships must not live only in (x,y) position — the tree already has first-class structure that a canvas should express, not replace.
mechanism: Position-as-only-record is the single most-cited reason infinite-canvas tools become 'write-only' once they grow past a small scale.
population: general knowledge-workers (product design convergence, practitioner essays, not controlled studies)

implications.text: Keep tree nodes first-class objects independent of layout position; the spatial view should default to a local view scoped to one document, not one canvas for every document ever fed in.

observation: Nielsen's progressive-disclosure guidance states more than two disclosure levels tends to have low usability, because users lose track of how many levels exist and how to get back — this directly conflicts with a naive 4-detent (L0-L3) dial.
claim: A flat 4-level dial risks a real usability cost; mitigation is keeping the breadcrumb to 2-3 visible ancestor levels and always labeling the current level with both name and a one-line description, not relying on the dial alone.
mechanism: Users lose track of how many disclosure levels exist and how navigation between them works once levels exceed about two.
population: general adults (UX practice, expert guidance not a single controlled study)

implications.text: Collapse deeper breadcrumb chains into an ellipsis (never show more than 2-3 ancestor levels at once); always show both the level name and a one-line description at the current level.

observation: Hornbæk & Frøkjær's controlled study of overview+detail vs. fisheye vs. detail-only found overview+detail produced significantly better essays (synthesis/comprehension) but was ~20% slower for targeted lookup tasks.
claim: A persistent minimap/overview should be dismissible rather than permanently forced on, since it helps synthesis tasks but costs time on lookup tasks.
mechanism: Split attention between overview and detail views trades comprehension gain for lookup speed, a genuine task-type-dependent tradeoff.
context: controlled study, primary source read only secondhand (403 blocked)

implications.text: Default the minimap on for first-time document opens (synthesis mode) and make it a rememberable per-user toggle for revisits (lookup mode).

observation: Landmark research (Vinson 1999; Sorrows & Hirtle 1999, via a 2021 review) converges on three necessary landmark properties: permanence (same place every time), uniqueness/visual distinctiveness, and identifiability (recognizable at a glance, not by reading).
claim: A landmark node in the abstraction tree needs a stable id/wording across regeneration and a small, deterministic, content-independent visual tag (color/icon from a hash of its id), not just a bolded heading.
mechanism: A landmark must be recognizable without reading it and must not change on revisit, or it fails the permanence/identifiability criteria that make navigation landmarks work.
population: general (virtual-environment navigation literature applied by analogy)
context: 2021 peer-reviewed literature review, applied by analogy to abstraction trees

implications.text: Assign each L1 node (and above-median-branching L2 node) a stable id and a deterministic, content-independent visual tag that persists across regeneration and zoom levels.

observation: `prefers-reduced-motion` (W3C Media Queries Level 5) is a settled, shipped, cross-browser standard specifically because scaling/zooming/parallax animation can induce vection-related nausea/disorientation in vestibular-disorder users; WebKit's guidance is to replace scaling/zooming with simpler alternatives like crossfade when the media query is set.
claim: All zoom-dial motion must be gated behind prefers-reduced-motion, with a crossfade-plus-instant-position-match fallback, not a partial or best-effort reduction.
mechanism: Large-scale visual movement across the field of view is the specific harm-causing pattern; color/opacity/blur changes are not motion in this sense, so a crossfade is a safe substitute.
population: general (vestibular-disorder-affected users; settled web accessibility standard)

implications.text: Implement a CSS media-query branch that replaces all zoom/pan animation with instant cut or crossfade under prefers-reduced-motion.

observation: Telescopic Text is a shipped, working implementation of word/clause-level stretchtext (click a highlighted span, it expands in place) with no published usability study, and Stretchtext itself (Ted Nelson, 1970) never reached mainstream adoption for the documented reason that a human author had to hand-write every nested version of the content.
claim: Riemann's LLM-generated levels remove the original authoring-cost blocker that kept 55-year-old stretchtext from spreading, which is a genuine structural reason to expect in-place level expansion to work now.
mechanism: Stretchtext's core interaction (expand in place, preserve surrounding context) was never shown to be wrong — it was blocked by the cost of manually authoring multiple content versions, a cost LLM generation removes.
population: general (historical/essayistic consensus on stretchtext's non-adoption, no controlled study)
context: historical hypertext systems and one live reference implementation

implications.text: Treat in-place, word/clause-level expansion as a viable interaction pattern worth prototyping, since the historical blocker (manual authoring) doesn't apply to Riemann's LLM-generated levels.
